questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute pH from hydrogen ion concentration
questions.stem: A solution has a hydrogen ion concentration of 1.0e-4 moles per litre. What is its pH? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, so negative log of 1.0e-4 is 4. The trap is using the natural logarithm or forgetting the negative sign, both of which produce very different numbers.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute hydrogen ion concentration from pH
questions.stem: A solution has pH 3.00. What is its hydrogen ion concentration in moles per litre? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen ion concentration is 10 to the negative pH, so 10 to the -3 is 0.001. A common trap is reporting pOH or using 10 to the positive pH.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: find pH of a strong acid solution
questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.010 moles per litre hydrochloric acid, assuming complete dissociation? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: HCl is a strong acid, so [H+] equals the acid concentration, 0.010, and negative log of 0.010 is 2. The trap is treating HCl as weak and using Ka.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute pOH from pH
questions.stem: A solution has pH 5.00 at 25 degrees Celsius. What is its pOH? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: At 25 degrees Celsius, pH plus pOH equals 14, so 14 minus 5 is 9. The trap is subtracting from 7 instead of 14.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute hydroxide concentration from pH
questions.stem: A solution has pH 10.00 at 25 degrees Celsius. What is its hydroxide ion concentration in moles per litre? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: pOH is 14 minus 10, or 4, so [OH-] is 10 to the -4, which is 0.0001. The trap is reporting [H+] instead of [OH-].

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: identify Brønsted-Lowry acid in a reaction
questions.stem: In the reaction NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH-, which species acts as the Brønsted-Lowry acid?

options.text: NH3, because it accepts a proton
options.misconception: Confuses a base with an acid

options.text: H2O, because it donates a proton
NH4+, because it is the conjugate acid
options.misconception: Selects a product instead of the reactant acid

options.text: OH-, because it is produced in the reaction
options.misconception: Confuses a product with an acid

questions.explanation: The Brønsted-Lowry acid donates a proton; here water donates a proton to ammonia. NH3 is the base, while NH4+ and OH- are products.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish strong and weak acids
questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a strong acid from a weak acid at the same concentration?

options.text: The strong acid has a higher hydrogen ion concentration
The strong acid has a larger molecular mass
The weak acid tastes less sour
The strong acid is always more concentrated

questions.explanation: Strength refers to degree of dissociation, so at equal concentration the strong acid produces more H+ and has lower pH. Concentration is a separate quantity.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute moles of acid needed for neutralization
questions.stem: How many moles of HCl are needed to neutralize 25.0 mL of 0.10 moles per litre NaOH? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Moles of NaOH are 0.0250 L times 0.10 mol/L, or 0.0025 mol. The one-to-one reaction needs the same moles of HCl. The trap is forgetting to convert millilitres to litres.
questions.hint: Moles = volume in litres times concentration.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute titrant volume at equivalence
questions.stem: What volume, in millilitres, of 0.10 moles per litre NaOH is needed to neutralize 25.0 mL of 0.20 moles per litre HCl? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Moles of HCl are 0.0250 L times 0.20 mol/L, or 0.0050 mol. Dividing by 0.10 mol/L NaOH gives 0.050 L, or 50 mL. The trap is assuming equal volumes.
questions.hint: Use moles of acid and base concentration.

questions.learningObjective: choose an indicator for a strong acid-strong base titration
questions.stem: Which indicator is most suitable for a strong acid–strong base titration?

options.text: Litmus, changing over a broad range

questions.explanation: A strong acid–strong base equivalence point is near pH 7, so an indicator changing near pH 7 is best. Phenolphthalein and methyl orange are more suited to titrations with equivalence points away from 7.
questions.hint: Match the indicator range to equivalence pH.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute buffer pH with equal acid and base
questions.stem: A buffer contains acetic acid and sodium acetate in equal amounts. The pKa of acetic acid is 4.76. What is the buffer pH? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation gives pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]). With equal amounts the ratio is 1, log of 1 is 0, so pH equals pKa, 4.76. The trap is adding log of 2.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute buffer pH from a 2:1 base-to-acid ratio
questions.stem: An acetic acid buffer has [CH3COO-]/[CH3COOH] = 2.0 and pKa = 4.76. What is the pH? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Using Henderson-Hasselbalch, pH = 4.76 + log(2.0) = 4.76 + 0.30 = 5.06. The trap is multiplying by 2 instead of taking the logarithm.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: predict buffer pH change after adding strong acid
questions.stem: What happens to the pH of an acetic acid/sodium acetate buffer when a small amount of HCl is added?

options.misconception: Reverses the effect of added acid

questions.explanation: Added H+ converts some acetate into acetic acid, slightly lowering pH, but the buffer resists large change. The pH does not stay fixed or become neutral.
questions.hint: Added acid consumes the base component.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute pH of a weak acid
questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.10 moles per litre acetic acid? Ka = 1.8e-5. Report the number only.
questions.explanation: For a weak acid, [H+] is approximately the square root of Ka times concentration: sqrt(1.8e-5 times 0.10) = 0.00134, giving pH 2.87. The trap is using the full acid concentration as [H+].

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute Kb of a conjugate base
questions.stem: An acid has Ka = 1.0e-5. What is Kb of its conjugate base? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Kb equals Kw divided by Ka, so 1.0e-14 divided by 1.0e-5 is 1.0e-9. The trap is multiplying Ka and Kw.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: classify a salt solution
questions.stem: An aqueous solution of sodium acetate is best described as:

options.misconception: Treats the anion as an acid

questions.explanation: Acetate is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it hydrolyzes water to produce OH-, making the solution basic. Sodium ion is a spectator.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute pH at equivalence for weak acid titration
questions.stem: At the equivalence point of titrating acetic acid with NaOH, the solution is 0.050 moles per litre sodium acetate. Kb for acetate is 5.6e-10. What is the pH? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Hydroxide concentration is approximately sqrt(Kb times 0.050) = 5.3e-6, so pOH is about 5.28 and pH is about 8.72. The equivalence point is basic because acetate hydrolyzes. The trap is assuming pH 7.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: relate equivalence volumes for a diprotic acid
questions.stem: During titration of a diprotic acid with a strong base, the second equivalence point occurs:

options.text: after twice the base volume needed for the first equivalence point
at the same base volume as the first equivalence point
only if the acid is strong
options.misconception: Confuses acid strength with proton count

questions.explanation: A diprotic acid has two acidic protons, so reaching the second equivalence point requires twice as much base as the first. Acid strength affects curve shape but not stoichiometry.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compute pH after dilution
questions.stem: A strong acid solution has pH 2.00. It is diluted by a factor of 10. What is the new pH? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: Diluting by a factor of 10 decreases [H+] by a factor of 10, so pH increases by 1, from 2 to 3. The trap is assuming pH scales linearly with volume.
questions.hint: pH changes by 1 per tenfold dilution.

questions.learningObjective: compare acid strength and concentration
questions.stem: A very dilute strong acid can have a higher pH than a concentrated weak acid. Is this statement true or false?

False, strong acids always have lower pH
True, because weak acids cannot donate protons
False, because concentration has no effect on pH

questions.explanation: pH depends on the actual hydrogen ion concentration. A dilute strong acid may produce less H+ than a concentrated weak acid, so its pH can be higher.

questions.stem: If a titration endpoint is reached after the equivalence point, the calculated analyte concentration is:
questions.explanation: An endpoint beyond equivalence means excess titrant volume was used. Since concentration is proportional to titrant volume, the calculated analyte concentration is too high.

questions.subject: CHEMISTRY
questions.learningObjective: compare Arrhenius and Brønsted-Lowry definitions
questions.stem: Ammonia is a base under the Brønsted-Lowry definition but not under the Arrhenius definition.

options.text: False, because ammonia produces OH- directly
options.misconception: Misstates how ammonia acts as base

options.text: False, because all bases contain OH-

questions.explanation: Arrhenius bases must produce OH- in water; ammonia does not contain or directly release OH-, but it accepts a proton, so it is a Brønsted-Lowry base. Thus the statement is true.
